title: The inevitable
hook: the reality, what is the reality (69:1–3)

segments.voice: Yesterday: no exception, the garden owners, and your line, the poor's share first. Today a new surah opens with one word, and then asks what it is.

Most of what fills a day isn't certain. The traffic might clear. The text might get a reply. The weather app says forty percent. We spend hours on maybes. Now think of the short list of things that are not maybes. The sun will set tonight. You were born. You will die. Surah sixty-nine is named for one thing on that list that is easy to forget. It opens by saying its name, and then asking what it is, twice.
screen: `A SURAH NAMED FOR ONE OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Surah al-Haqqah begins, in Pickthall's translation: "The Reality! What is the Reality?" Then the third verse asks again: and what will make you know what the Reality is? Al-haqqah comes from the root h-q-q, the root of haqq: truth, what is real, what is due, what must come to pass. Translators reach for different words, the Reality, the Inevitable, the Sure Truth, because the Arabic holds all of them. One of the names of Allah, al-Haqq, the Truth, the Real, comes from the same root. The opening is a teaching device the Qur'an uses more than once: name a thing, ask what it is, then ask how you could possibly know. And what is it? Commentators read it as the Day of Resurrection, the day that is certain to come. But the surah doesn't open with a description. It goes straight into history: the peoples of 'Ad and Thamud, who called the coming day a lie, and what happened to them. Pharaoh. The flood in Nuh's time. Before telling you about the day, the surah reminds you that people have been sure it wasn't coming for a very long time. The point isn't fear for its own sake. It's sorting. Some things in your life are maybes. A few are haqq, real and due. The surah's opening is a call to tell them apart.

Let today's maybes come up, the worries, the plans, the waiting, and set each one to the side, as if on a shelf. Then ask what's certain: that I'm breathing now, that this day will end, that my life will end too, one day, and, Muslims would add, that I'll be asked what I did with it. Stay with that short list, and notice how quiet it is.
The inevitable. Al-Haqqah, the Reality: the day that is certain to come, from the root of haqq, what is true and due. Today's word.
Your line: what is real. A few things are due; the rest are maybes. Day six hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims believe in the Last Day as one of the articles of faith; surahs like al-Haqqah, recited in prayer, are a regular reminder of it, and al-Haqq, the Truth, is one of the names of Allah.
